text.p: Imperial Chemical Industries Plc's first-half results on July 24 will carry a strong sense of anti-climax after weeks of hectic reinvention by the British group.

ICI told the markets on Monday this week that its interim pre-tax profits had plunged to 160 million stg from 367 million a year earlier, hit by continued sharp falls in prices for polymers and tioxide and the rampaging pound.
It said these factors had more than offset strong sales volumes and productivity savings.

The figures were published as ICI announced it had offloaded both of these underperforming bulk chemical operations to DuPont Co of the U.S. for $3 billion, a major milestone in its efforts to recast itself as a high-margin, speciality chemical company.

Analysts said the figures graphically illustrated ICI's motivation for a switch out of bulk products and into consumer-led areas such as industrial adhesives, catalysts, acrylic monomers and food flavourings.
Thursday's results will be the last shout of the old ICI, with $8 billion of new businesses acquired from Unilever Plc starting to contribute in the second half of the year.
The switch is expected to lead to a much higher quality and more stable stream of earnings.
"The bulk chemical industry's profitability is significantly more volatile historically," UBS bond credit research analyst Matthew Taylor said in a note on Thursday.

The share price has continued to surge following news of last week's disposal to DuPont, at prices which surprised most observers. Analysts said this helped to alleviate some concerns, inside ICI as well as outside, that the group had overpaid for the Unilever businesses.

Late morning on Friday, ICI was trading at 928 pence after touching a 12-month high of 934 pence, a gain of 14 percent since the DuPont sale was announced on Monday and 30 percent since the May 7 deal with Unilever.

Some analysts believe the share will reach 10 stg in the next few weeks, although others are arguing that around eight pounds is fairer value for a company which still has half its bulk chemicals to dispose of and hefty debts.
